title: Freedom of Information
hook: You can't hold power to account for what you can't see. Freedom of information laws pry open the workings of government so citizens can actually check it.
key_points: Freedom of information (FOI) is the public's right to access records held by government.
It rests on the principle that official information belongs to the public, with limited exceptions.
Transparency deters wrongdoing and enables real oversight and informed debate.
Exceptions (security, privacy) exist but can be misused to hide embarrassment.
content_html: Accountability depends on information: citizens, journalists, and watchdogs can only scrutinize what government actually does if they can find out what it is doing. Freedom of information (FOI) turns that requirement into a right — the legally recognized ability of the public to request and receive records held by public bodies. Its underlying principle is a quiet but powerful reversal of old assumptions about official secrecy: government information is presumed to belong to the public it serves, and should be open by default, with secrecy the exception that must be justified rather than the norm.
extra_html: Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that freedom-of-information laws have spread widely as a tool of open and accountable government. Their value is practical. Transparency deters wrongdoing — officials behave differently when they know their decisions and spending can be examined — and it supplies the raw material for genuine oversight and informed public debate, complementing a free press and formal watchdog institutions. FOI is, in effect, the supply line for accountability. Of course, not all information can be open: legitimate exceptions protect things like national security, ongoing investigations, and personal privacy. But these exceptions are also the system's weak point, because they can be stretched. A government reluctant to be embarrassed may invoke "security" or "confidentiality" to withhold information that is merely inconvenient rather than genuinely sensitive. The ongoing challenge of FOI is therefore to keep the presumption of openness strong and the exceptions narrow and well-policed — so that secrecy protects the public interest rather than shielding power from scrutiny.

related.title: Accountability & Oversight
related.hook: Power left unwatched drifts toward abuse. Accountability is the demand that officials answer for what they do — and oversight is the machinery that makes them.

related.title: Political Corruption
related.hook: Corruption is the abuse of entrusted power for private gain — and it quietly drains a society, eroding trust, fairness, and the resources meant for everyone.

related.title: The Free Press & Democracy
related.hook: A free press is sometimes called the "fourth estate" — an unofficial branch of power whose job is to watch the other three on the public's behalf.
